title: Arapahoe County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Arapahoe County wells have a 176 ft median depth. Review local yields, water levels, drilling costs and risks before buying land or building.
h1: What to Expect from a Well in Arapahoe County
intro_html:
A well budget in Arapahoe County starts with the parcel, not the county average. The median recorded depth is 176 ft, but the middle half runs from 32-480 ft. That spread matters when pricing land near Strasburg or comparing a well property in Foxfield with one near Aurora.

Colorado DWR records contain 16,238 county well permits, with 8,148 recorded as constructed. These are not all household supplies: monitoring accounts for 30% of the use mix. Use the county figures to get oriented, then check nearby completed wells serving the same purpose as yours.

sections.heading: Why Arapahoe County's Median Depth Is Not a Bid
sections.html:
Of the 9,158 wells reporting depth, the median is 176 ft. The middle half spans 32-480 ft, and the 90th percentile reaches 780 ft. That is too wide a range to price a new household well from the median alone. A bid should identify the intended aquifer and explain how additional footage will be charged.

The cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. Permits name the Denver aquifer on 2,387 wells and the Arapahoe on 1,336. Another 8,671 carry an unnamed / fractured-bedrock aquifer label, which does not establish parcel geology. Compare construction logs around Foxfield, Aurora or Strasburg rather than assuming those locations share a drilling target.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Are Generally Useful, Not Guaranteed
sections.html:
The 3,465 wells with pump-yield records have a median of 12.0 gpm, with a middle half of 10.0-15.0 gpm. Those reported rates are encouraging for household supply, but they are not a promise of sustained production from a particular lot. A completion-test yield and a current pumping test answer different questions.

The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, while 2% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. Do not read that as proof that low-producing or unsuccessful wells are absent; the yield summary only covers wells with reported measurements. Before buying, have the existing well evaluated for sustained output and recovery, and confirm that the permit allows your intended use.

sections.heading: Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Countywide Decline
sections.html:
Static water level means depth to resting water, not total drilled depth. Among 763 reporting wells, the median is 88 ft below ground and the middle half is 27-218 ft. That helps frame pumping conditions, but pump selection also needs the water level while the well is operating.

The decade medians do not establish a steadily dropping water table. They deepen from 34 ft in the 1950s to 250 ft in the 1990s, then shift to 28 ft in the 2000s, 110 ft in the 2010s and 95 ft in the 2020s. These are grouped measurements, not repeated readings from the same wells. Ask for a property's own water-level and pumping history before drawing a depletion conclusion.

sections.heading: Arapahoe's Permit History and Recorded Drillers
sections.html:
Permit issuance reached 3,287 in the 2000s, compared with 2,852 in the 1990s and 1,889 in the 2010s. The records include 1,141 permits from the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. That last decade is incomplete, and permit issuance is not the same as completed construction.

Prominent drilling entries include Crandall Drilling & Pump Service (Crandall Jr., Howard H.), with 1,014 records, and Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.), with 864. The largest listed entry, Authorized (Pe, Pg), has 3,068 records but is an authorization-style label rather than a clear company name. Historical record counts do not confirm current availability or suitability for your parcel.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well in Denver Basin Bedrock
sections.html:
The drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the county's 176 ft median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $8,800-$12,300. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $14,800-$24,300.

Those are median-depth planning figures, not a parcel quote. With the middle half of recorded depths reaching from 32-480 ft, footage can materially change the total. Ask the contractor to separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, trenching and electrical. Confirm access requirements and what happens if the planned depth does not produce an acceptable supply. Septic construction and broader site development need their own budgets.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and the Whole Building Site
sections.html:
The mapped environmental inventory within about 10 miles includes 646 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 168 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 6 historic mine features. These counts flag the need for parcel-level review; they do not show that a particular well is contaminated. Sampling locations and confirmed contamination are not interchangeable.

For an existing well, obtain laboratory water testing and choose additional analyses based on nearby site records. Review casing, grout, wellhead drainage and the septic layout. For a new build, establish workable well and septic locations before fixing the house footprint. Neither a permit nor favorable neighboring yields guarantees a productive hole, so address low yield and unsuccessful drilling in the contract.

sections.heading: Before Closing on a Foxfield or Strasburg Lot
sections.html:
Start with the actual permit, completion report and parcel boundaries. Arapahoe County's use mix includes 44% domestic/household, 14% stock and 7% irrigation; a nearby well's existence does not establish your right to those uses. DWR permit conditions control, and household-use authorization should not be treated as permission for outdoor watering.

Compare nearby wells with similar permitted uses and aquifer targets, then ask a driller to review the logs against your building plan. Keep driveway access, drilling access, septic placement and utility trench routes in the same site discussion. For an existing home, obtain a current pumping test and water-quality results before closing rather than relying only on the original permit record.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Arapahoe County?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 176 ft, and the middle half runs from 32-480 ft. The 90th percentile is 780 ft. Because the county records include monitoring wells and other uses, those figures are a starting point, not a household-well specification. Nearby construction logs and the intended aquifer are better guides for a parcel-specific drilling estimate.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Arapahoe County?
faq.a: The model uses $50-$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 176 ft median depth, the drilled hole is about $8,800-$12,300, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $14,800-$24,300. Actual depth, construction requirements and site access can change the quote. Ask for itemized scope and additional-footage terms.

faq.q: How much water do Arapahoe County wells produce?
faq.a: Among 3,465 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gpm and the middle half is 10.0-15.0 gpm. The reported 1-5 gpm share is 2%. These records are useful for comparison, but they do not establish a property's current sustained supply. Get a pumping and recovery test before relying on an existing well for a purchase.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Arapahoe County?
faq.a: County permit statistics cannot establish drinking-water safety. The nearby mapped inventory includes 646 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 168 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, but proximity does not prove a well is affected. Obtain laboratory testing for the property, review relevant environmental records, and inspect the wellhead and septic setting. Choose additional testing based on the identified local concerns.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Arapahoe County?
faq.a: The provided decade medians do not demonstrate a steady countywide decline. Median depth to water was 250 ft in the 1990s, 28 ft in the 2000s and 95 ft in the 2020s. Those groups are not a same-well monitoring series. A property's repeated water-level measurements and pumping history are more useful for judging changes in its supply.
